title: Snooze control: Apple Watch helps data-track your way to a better sleep

extractedText: In a city that treats grind culture like a competitive sport, actually getting eight hours of sleep can feel less like a health choice and more like a radical act of rebellion. But as we head into World Sleep Day on March 13, it’s time to admit that a successful hustle is only as good as our REM cycle. Sleep matters – and so does tracking it. Thanks to new updates, the Apple Health team has turned Apple’s beloved wrist candy into a high-tech sleep lap. Guided by Dr. Matt Bianchi, a board-certified neurologist and sleep expert, Apple makes it simple to data track your way to a better morning via the Apple Watch. See more: 4 Magic Sleeping Positions to Help You Sleep Better Photo: Courtesy From when to how In the landscape of wearable health tech, Apple has moved beyond tracking when we sleep to how we sleep – and what that means for our long-term clinical health. The Apple Watch (Series 11, Ultra 3, and SE 3) utilizes a multi-sensor approach to determine sleep quality. Dr. Bianchi, a research scientist on Apple’s Health Technologies team, is at the centre of this tech revolution. A neurologist who still maintains a clinical practice at the Stanford Sleep Clinic, Dr. Bianchi is the bridge between Silicon Valley sensors and actual medical science. ADVERTISEMENT One of the biggest hurdles he faces? Correcting our misconceptions about what a “good” night actually looks like. “One myth has to do with the focus on REM sleep and deep sleep,” Dr. Bianchi explains. “Some people think they are the most important aspects of sleep, whereas in the clinical and research evidence, sleep duration and consistency of schedule are far more important.” Photo: Pexels The intelligence behind the zzz’s To get the data right, Dr. Bianchi and his team pioneered sensor fusion, which combines accelerometer data (movement) with heart rate and respiratory sensors. This allows the watch to estimate time spent in REM, Core, and Deep sleep. Photo: Courtesy However, Dr. Bianchi’s real contribution is shifting the focus to longitudinal tracking – the idea that one bad night isn’t a crisis, but a month of data is a roadmap. The Apple Watch can identify patterns – and deviations in patterns – over weeks and months to reduce bias and uncertainty. ADVERTISEMENT “I think of them as connected,” Dr. Bianchi says of the relationship between routine and rest. “In the Apple Heart and Movement Study, we looked at tens of thousands of people, and the folks with the most consistent timing of sleep were actually getting more sleep – about 40-minutes more on average – than the least consistent group.” Photo: Courtesy New & critical Apple Watch features in 2026 If you haven’t checked your Health app lately or updated your operating system, you’re missing out on a sophisticated toolkit to a better night’s sleep. “Good sleep doesn’t mean zero awakenings at night.”Dr. Bianchi Sleep Score Released with watchOS 26, this assigns a 1-100 value based on duration, consistency, and restorative stages. It’s calculated using duration, consistency, and how many times you were startled awake by a neighbour’s car alarm or restless partner. And if you’re the type to stress over every wake-up, Dr. Bianchi has good news: “Good sleep doesn’t mean zero awakenings at night. It turns out being awake sometimes is perfectly normal… You can still get a perfect score with a certain number of awakenings,” says Dr. Bianchi. The Vitals App Acting as an early warning system, this dedicated app establishes a typical range for your overnight metrics. It tracks heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature, and blood oxygen while you sleep. If two or more of these metrics fall outside your typical range, you’ll get a notification the next morning – often a sign that an illness or a high-stress day is in store. ADVERTISEMENT “It’s a ‘you versus you’ comparison,” says Dr. Bianchi. “When we surface the notification, we say up front this is not designed to be an illness detector… but when you see outliers, it might be from an illness, exercise, alcohol, or other factors, just to help the person make those connections.” Apple Watch users can track their sleep and receive insights into sleep quality with sleep score, receive insights on heart health including hypertension notifications, track their menstrual cycle, and more. (Photo: Courtesy) Hypertension Notifications Included in the latest Series 11 models, this feature monitors for signs of chronic high blood pressure, often a byproduct of poor sleep. Because hypertension is often “silent,” the watch looks for physiological markers during your most restful hours to identify risks that might otherwise go unnoticed until a formal check-up. Sleep Apnea Notifications This feature, which received FDA 510(k) clearance in late 2024, uses an algorithm to detect breathing disturbances, specifically hypopneas and apneas.
